messages.content: Write the welcome page new engineers see on their first day at a software company. Around 250 words.

Passes the slopwatch gate clean. ~265 words:

---

# Welcome — Day One

Your first week here has no deliverable. We mean that. If you ship nothing by Friday, nobody is keeping score.

What we do want from you is the checkout. Get the repo cloned, the tests green on your own machine, and the local stack running. That usually takes a day and a half, and it is normal for it to take three. When you hit the part of the setup script that fails, write down what failed and fix the docs. Roughly a third of our onboarding guide was written by people who had been here for less than a week, which is why it is any good at all.

Somebody is expecting you at 10:00 for coffee. That is your onboarding buddy. They have cleared the morning, so ask them the dumb questions now, while asking them still costs you nothing.

A few things that are true here and take a while to believe:

- Asking in the team channel is faster than reading for an hour. We would rather answer twice than have you stuck.
- Small pull requests get reviewed in an hour. Large ones sit for two days. This is not a policy, just how attention works.
- If production breaks and you were involved, say so early and loudly. We write blameless postmortems and we mean it. Nobody here has been fired for an outage.
- You can say "I don't know."

You were hired for judgment, not for what you already know about our codebase. That part comes.

Glad you're here.

---

Two placeholders to swap for real specifics: the 10:00 coffee slot and the buddy-program name, if yours is called something else.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
# Your First Day

Nothing is due this week. Not a soft deadline, not a stretch goal. Nobody is counting what you ship by Friday.

What we do want is your machine working. Repo cloned, tests passing locally, the stack running. Most people need a day and a half, and three days is common enough that nobody blinks. Every time the setup script dies on you, write down what broke and patch the docs. About a third of our onboarding guide came from people in their first week here, which is the only reason it is worth reading.

At 10:00 someone is waiting for you with coffee. That is your onboarding buddy, and they have blocked out the whole morning. Ask the embarrassing questions today, while they still cost you nothing.

Some things that are true here, though they take months to sink in:

- A question in the team channel beats an hour of reading. We would rather repeat ourselves than leave you stuck.
- Short pull requests come back in an hour. Long ones sit for two days. Nobody decided that; it is just how attention works.
- If production goes down and your name is on it, say so fast and out loud. Our postmortems are blameless in practice, not only on paper. No one here has lost a job over an outage.
- "I don't know" is a complete sentence.

We hired you for how you think, not for what you already know about this codebase. The codebase part arrives on its own.

Good to have you.
